intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NDUFV2 gene (600532) on chromosome 18p11.

paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation in the NDUFV2 gene, which encodes a subunit of mitochondrial complex I. Patients reported by Bénit et al. (2003) and Cameron et al. (2015) had early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with trunk hypotonia, encephalopathy, or brain atrophy. Cameron et al. (2015) also described a family with Leigh syndrome and no cardiac involvement.

paragraphs.text: In 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous family with complex I deficiency and early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Bénit et al. (2003) used denaturing HPLC and sequencing to identify a homozygous 4-bp deletion in intron 2 of the NDUFV2 gene (IVS2+5_+8delGTAA). The deletion altered the consensus splice-donor site of exon 2 and resulted in a 70% decrease in NDUFV2 protein and complex I deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Cameron et al. (2015) performed whole-exome sequencing on fibroblast DNA from 1 of 2 sibs with complex I deficiency, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and brain atrophy, filtering for novel nonsynonymous changes. They found compound heterozygous mutations in the NDUFV2 gene. One was a previously reported intronic splice mutation, which they designated c.IVS2+1delGTAA and considered disease causing. The other was a novel 1-bp insertion (c.669_670insG) predicted to cause a frameshift (p.Ser224Valfs*3).

paragraphs.text: Pagniez-Mammeri et al. (2009) screened 8 patients with biochemically proven isolated mitochondrial complex I deficiency for mutations in 8 nuclear complex I genes, including NDUFV2. They used Surveyor nuclease digestion of 22 cDNA fragments covering the coding sequences. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms and missense mutations were detected in 18.7% of the cDNA fragments, and molecular defects were identified in 3 patients. The authors concluded that Surveyor nuclease screening of cDNAs is a reliable and easy-to-interpret way to genotype nuclear complex I deficiencies and that it reduces the number of sequencing reactions needed. They suggested that the method would make prenatal diagnosis more feasible.
